To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a loop of neurones in the cerebellar nuclei (the output nuclei of the cerebellum) and in the reticular nuclei of the brain stem (the main source of descending commands to the spinal cord) is involved in the execution of voluntary movements and in the correction of any errors made in this process.

the cerebellum is able to detect the degree of inhibition that is applied to motoneurones, and that this information is conveyed to the cerebellum by neurones located in the reticular nucleus in the brainstem.

1) The cerebellum is informed about the likelihood of the brain's commands being executed as planned, 2) The information is conveyed from the brainstem to the cerebellum via the spinal cord and, 3) The information is provided by spinal neurones, which are inhibited by the descending reticulosphinal neurones.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms by which the spinal cord contributes to the execution of voluntary movements and to the control of the brain's commands.
the neural mechanisms that underlie the ability of the brain to control the body.
the neural mechanisms underlying the control and coordination of movement.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this study provides evidence that the trans‐spinal pathway between the cerebellar nuclei and the reticular formation may provide an important link in the cerebellar control of motor activity.
the trans‐spinal cerebellar‐reticulospinal pathway provides an important link between the cerebellum and the brain's ability to execute voluntary movements.

this study demonstrates a trans‐spinal cerebellar‐reticular‐cerebellar loop that provides the cerebellum (and probably the brain) with a continuous assessment of the likelihood that descending commands are being executed correctly.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we show a trans‐spinal feedback loop that provides information to the brain about the likelihood of the spinal cord's response to the brain's signals being correct.

the brain has a direct access to the spinal cord, but the spinal cord also has a direct access back to the brain, and that this access is used to correct the brain's signals to the spinal motor system.
the brain is continuously informed about how likely it is to achieve its goals.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we found that there are neurones in the spinal cord that provide information to the cerebellum on the degree to which the brain's descending commands are being implemented in the spinal cord.
the brain and the cerebellum are in constant dialogue about how well the brain's commands will be executed in the spinal cord, and the cerebellar output may be used to adjust those commands.
the brain is able to monitor its own signals to the spinal motor centres, and to correct them if necessary.
